blocks.text: An abacus is a counting tool. It is a frame with rods, and on each rod there are beads that slide up and down. Each rod stands for a different amount. The first rod counts ones. blocks.prompt: Counting Before Calculators
blocks.text: Long before anyone had a calculator, people needed a fast way to add and subtract. One of the best tools they invented was the abacus. An abacus is a wooden frame filled with rods, and on each rod sit beads that slide back and forth. What makes it clever is that each rod stands for a different place value. One rod is the ones, the next is the tens, the next is the hundreds, and so on. To show the number 24, you slide two beads on the tens rod and four beads on the ones rod. The abacus is thousands of years old. Merchants in ancient China, Rome, and the Middle East all used counting boards or bead frames to keep track of money. The Chinese version is called a suanpan. A skilled user can move the beads so quickly that the abacus keeps up with a modern calculator for adding and subtracting. It never runs out of battery, and it never needs to be plugged in.

blocks.prompt: One Bead Worth Five
blocks.text: The abacus is one of the oldest calculating tools ever made, and it is still taught in schools today. At first it looks simple: a frame, some rods, and rows of beads that slide. But the design hides a clever idea. Each rod stands for a place value, ones on the right, then tens, then hundreds, so a small number of beads can represent a huge number. The Japanese abacus, called a soroban, is even more efficient. A bar divides each rod into two parts. Below the bar sit four beads, and each one is worth one. Above the bar sits a single bead worth five. That means one rod can show any digit from zero to nine using only five beads. To read the number, you look at which beads have been pushed toward the middle bar. The real surprise is what happens after a child practices for a while. Because the fingers always move the beads in the same patterns, the brain starts to picture the beads without the frame. Expert students can put the physical abacus away and calculate by imagining the beads moving in their mind. This skill is called mental abacus, and children trained in it can add long lists of numbers faster than most adults can with a calculator. An ancient tool made of wood and beads turns out to be an excellent way to teach a modern brain how numbers work.

blocks.prompt: The Counting Board and the Pebble
blocks.text: The abacus may be the oldest calculating device still in use, and its story is tangled up with the history of numbers themselves. The word abacus probably comes from the Greek abax, meaning a board or a flat surface. That word may reach back even further to a Semitic word for dust, because the earliest counting boards were trays of fine sand or dust in which a merchant drew lines and marked figures with a finger. When the marks were wiped away, the board was ready for the next sum. Later, people set loose pebbles on the lines of the board instead of drawing. The Romans called those little stones calculi, and the beads on rods that we picture today grew out of that idea. We still carry the Roman pebble around in our language: the words calculate and calculator both come from calculus, the Latin word for a small stone. What makes the abacus powerful is place value. Each rod, line, or column stands for a different size of number: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. A handful of beads arranged across a few rods can therefore stand for a number in the millions. The tool does not do the thinking for you. It holds the number steady while your hands and eyes do the work, which frees your mind to move on to the next step. That is also why the abacus does something a calculator cannot. After enough practice, a trained student no longer needs the frame at all. The pattern of the beads becomes so familiar that it can be pictured in the mind, and calculations are carried out on an imaginary abacus. This mental version is called anzan, and champions can add dozens of numbers in seconds, faster than a hand can press the keys of a calculator. An object first used to escape the limits of memory ends up training memory to work without it.

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Machine We Still Use
blocks.text: An abacus is, at heart, a machine for holding a number still. It is nothing more than a frame, a set of rods or wires, and beads that slide along them, yet that simple arrangement is one of the most successful pieces of technology humans have ever built. Versions of it have been in continuous use for more than two thousand years, which is longer than almost any tool you could name. Its history runs alongside the history of counting itself. The word abacus probably comes from the Greek abax, a board or slab, and that word may trace back to a Semitic term for dust. The connection is not an accident. The earliest counting boards were flat trays covered in fine sand, and a trader would draw lines in the sand and push marks around to add and subtract, wiping the surface clean when the sum was done. In time the drawn marks became loose counters, and the Romans set small stones in the grooves of their boards. They called those stones calculi. We have never let go of the word: calculate, calculator, and even the medical calculus that forms in a body all descend from the Latin for a little pebble. The idea that makes the whole thing work is place value. Each rod stands for a different order of magnitude, ones, then tens, then hundreds, then thousands, so a mere handful of beads can pin down a number in the millions. Different cultures refined the layout. The Chinese suanpan gives each rod two beads above the dividing bar and five below it. The Japanese soroban streamlined this to one bead above and four below, which is all you need to show any digit from zero to nine. In every version, a number is not written down but built, physically, with the hands. The abacus does not calculate for you. It stores the number so your mind is free to work on the next move. That physical quality leads to the strangest part of the story. A child who drills on a soroban long enough stops needing it. The hand movements and the picture of the sliding beads become so deeply learned that the frame can be taken away entirely, and the calculation runs on an abacus that exists only in the mind. This is called anzan, and its results are hard to believe: trained students glance at a screen flashing a dozen three-digit numbers for a fraction of a second each and announce the total before an adult could even reach for a calculator. Brain scans of these students suggest they are not using the language part of the mind that most of us use for arithmetic. They are using the parts that handle vision and movement, as though they really are watching and touching beads that are not there. That is why an ancient frame of wood and beads has survived into the age of the smartphone. A calculator gives you an answer and tells you nothing. An abacus makes the structure of a number visible and physical, so a child does not just find the answer but sees why it is the answer. The tool was invented to reach past the limits of human memory, and it ended up teaching human memory to do the work alone.
